# Workshop Series: Website Launch Communication Strategy

## Overview

Five half-day workshops (3 hours each), designed to build progressively from audience insight to a fully actionable launch communication plan. Each session produces a concrete deliverable that feeds into the next.

**Recommended cadence:** One workshop per week, with 2–3 days of async reflection between sessions.

**Ideal participants:** Product/stakeholder lead, marketing lead, content lead, design lead, engineering lead, one representative from each key audience segment (or a proxy), and a facilitator. Cap the room at 8–12 people.

---

## Workshop 1 — Audience & Discovery
**Goal:** Define *who* the launch communication is for and what they need to hear.

| Time | Activity | Technique |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00–0:20 | Framing & objectives | Talk-through of the website's purpose, goals, and success criteria |
| 0:20–1:00 | Stakeholder & audience mapping | **Stakeholder mapping** (power/interest grid) + **personas** (3–5 segments) |
| 1:00–1:40 | Needs & pain-point exploration | **Empathy mapping** per persona — what do they know, feel, need, and fear about the current site vs. the new one? |
| 1:40–2:00 | Break | — |
| 2:00–2:40 | Prioritise audiences | **Dot-voting** to rank the top 3 audiences by reach × impact |
| 2:40–3:00 | Synthesis & next steps | Assign owners to validate personas with quick research (interviews, analytics) before Workshop 2 |

**Output:** Audience map with 3 prioritised personas, each with goals, pain points, and information needs.

---

## Workshop 2 — Messaging & Positioning
**Goal:** Agree on *what* we say and *why* it matters.

| Time | Activity | Technique |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00–0:15 | Recap & research findings | Share async research from Workshop 1 homework |
| 0:15–1:00 | Value proposition workshop | **Value Proposition Canvas** — map audience pains/gains to the website's features and benefits |
| 1:00–1:40 | Core message architecture | **Message house** — 1 big idea → 3 supporting pillars → 3–4 proof points each |
| 1:40–2:00 | Break | — |
| 2:00–2:30 | Tone & voice calibration | **Tone spectrum exercise** — plot 5–6 axes (formal↔casual, bold↔reassuring, technical↔accessible) and agree on the brand's position |
| 2:30–3:00 | Message testing & refinement | Read messages aloud; apply the **"So what?"** test three times to sharpen each pillar |

**Output:** A one-page message architecture (big idea, pillars, proof points) and a tone-of-voice guide.

---

## Workshop 3 — Channels & Tactics
**Goal:** Decide *where* and *how* each audience hears the message.

| Time | Activity | Technique |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00–0:15 | Recap | Review message architecture |
| 0:15–1:00 | Channel inventory | **Channel audit** — list every owned, earned, and paid channel available; score each for reach, cost, and fit per persona |
| 1:00–1:40 | Channel-to-audience matching | **Mapping matrix** — plot personas (rows) × channels (columns); fill in the specific tactic for each cell (e.g., email teaser, in-app banner, LinkedIn post, press release) |
| 1:40–2:00 | Break | — |
| 2:00–2:30 | Content & asset planning | **Content inventory table** — for each tactic, define format, owner, and rough word count / length |
| 2:30–3:00 | Gap & dependency check | Identify what's missing (assets, approvals, vendor access) and flag risks |

**Output:** A channel-by-audience tactic matrix with assigned content formats and owners.

---

## Workshop 4 — Timeline, Roles & Execution Plan
**Goal:** Turn the strategy into a *when, who, and how* plan.

| Time | Activity | Technique |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00–0:15 | Recap | Review tactic matrix |
| 0:15–1:00 | Launch timeline build | **Backward timeline / critical-path mapping** — start from launch day and work back through pre-launch (teasers, embargo lift, press), launch day, and post-launch (sustained comms) |
| 1:00–1:40 | Roles & RACI | **RACI matrix** for every tactic — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed |
| 1:40–2:00 | Break | — |
| 2:00–2:30 | Approval & dependency workflow | Map sign-off stages (legal, brand, engineering) onto the timeline; identify the longest lead-time items |
| 2:30–3:00 | Dry-run & contingency | **Pre-mortem** — "It's launch day and the plan has failed. Why?" Capture top 5 risks and mitigation steps |

**Output:** A Gantt-style launch timeline, a RACI table, and a risk register with mitigations.

---

## Workshop 5 — Measurement, Readiness & Sign-Off
**Goal:** Define success, confirm readiness, and lock the plan.

| Time | Activity | Technique |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 0:00–0:20 | Recap & alignment check | Quick walk-through of the full strategy; surface any misalignments |
| 0:20–1:00 | KPI & measurement design | **Balanced scorecard** — set 1–2 KPIs per objective (awareness, engagement, conversion, sentiment) with baseline, target, and data source |
| 1:00–1:30 | Feedback & iteration loop | Design the post-launch review cadence (day 1, week 1, month 1) and the "what do we change?" decision framework |
| 1:30–1:50 | Break | — |
| 1:50–2:30 | Launch-day runbook | Build a **minute-by-minute launch-day script** (who says what, when, to whom) for the go-live moment |
| 2:30–3:00 | Sign-off & celebration | Final review of all five deliverables; assign a single strategy owner; agree on a "go/no-go" checkpoint date |

**Output:** KPI dashboard spec, post-launch review plan, launch-day runbook, and a signed-off strategy document.

---

## Facilitation Tips Across All Workshops

- **Park the lot:** Keep a visible "parking lot" for ideas that don't fit the current session; revisit at the end of each workshop.
- **Decide, don't discuss:** Use dot-voting or consensus checks to close every activity. Avoid open-ended "anyone want to add?" loops.
- **Capture live:** Have a scribe (or shared Miro/FigJam board) documenting decisions in real time so participants see the strategy taking shape.
- **Homework between sessions:** Each workshop ends with 2–3 specific research or drafting tasks assigned to named owners, due before the next session.
- **Start every session with a 5-minute "what changed?" check-in** to surface new information, blockers, or scope shifts since the last meeting.

---

## Final Deliverable

After Workshop 5, the team holds a single **Website Launch Communication Strategy** document containing:

1. Audience personas & priorities
2. Message architecture & tone guide
3. Channel × audience tactic matrix
4. Launch timeline with RACI
5. Risk register & mitigations
6. KPI dashboard & review cadence
7. Launch-day runbook

This becomes the living reference for the launch team and the handoff point for execution.

Want me to drill deeper into any single workshop — for example, a detailed facilitator script, specific slide prompts, or an adapted version for a smaller team or a different launch context (B2B SaaS, e-commerce, internal tool)?

# Fail-Fast Funnel: Weekly Evaluation of Open-Weight Model Releases

## 1. Purpose and Constraints

Each week, one or more new open-weight models appear (new releases, fine-tunes, quantised variants, architecture changes). This document defines a single-machine evaluation pipeline that **rejects the obvious failures in minutes** and spends its scarce GPU-hours only on candidates that survive every cheaper gate.

Hard constraints the design must respect:

| Constraint | Implication |
|---|---|
| **One machine** | Total weekly GPU budget is fixed (assume ~40 GPU-hours). Every stage must have a hard time cap. |
| **Weekly cadence** | At most one full evaluation cycle per week. Anything that can't finish in a week is deferred, not run. |
| **Open weights** | We can download, load, and inspect the model directly. No API dependency. |
| **Fail-fast** | Stages are ordered by cost. A candidate that fails stage *k* never reaches stage *k+1*. |

The funnel is not a ranking system. It is a **gatekeeper**: each stage answers one yes/no question — *"is this model worth spending more compute on?"* — and the cheapest test that can answer "no" is the one that runs.

---

## 2. The Stages

Five stages, each with a fixed time budget, a mechanical disqualifier, and a promotion criterion. A candidate either advances or is logged as rejected with the specific evidence.

### Stage 0 — Metadata Triage
**Budget: 0 minutes of GPU. ~10 minutes of reading.**

What runs: a script pulls the model card, `config.json`, tokenizer files, and the HuggingFace / repo metadata. No model is loaded.

**Cheapest disqualifiers (checked in this order):**

1. **License.** Is the license compatible with your deployment and distribution constraints? (e.g., an "AI-Only" or research-only license disqualifies a model you need in a commercial product.) This is a string match against a maintained allow-list.
2. **Architecture / precision.** Can your hardware actually load it? If the model requires a tensor-parallel layout across 8 GPUs, or ships only in FP8 with no GGUF/AWQ variant, it's out on a single machine.
3. **Context window.** If your workload requires ≥ 32k tokens and the model's `max_position_embeddings` is 4k, disqualify.
4. **Provenance.** Is the checkpoint a verified release from the stated organisation, or an unverified re-upload? Unverified provenance → reject (this is a supply-chain check, not a quality check).

**Promotion criterion:** all four checks pass. The candidate enters the download queue.

> *Why this stage exists:* most "new releases" that appear in a week are quantised variants, LoRA adapters for models you already evaluated, or re-uploads. Stage 0 filters those out for free.

---

### Stage 1 — Loadability and Smoke Test
**Budget: 15 minutes of GPU. 5 prompts.**

What runs: download the weights, load the model into memory (or VRAM), and generate 5 completions from a fixed smoke-test prompt set:

- a one-sentence factual question with a known answer,
- a simple arithmetic problem,
- a "repeat the following exactly" instruction (tests instruction-following plumbing),
- a prompt in a non-English language,
- a prompt that should produce a short, structured output (e.g., "list 3 items as JSON").

**Cheapest disqualifiers:**

1. **Load failure.** The model doesn't load, OOMs, or the tokenizer is mismatched (garbage token IDs). → Reject.
2. **Gibberish.** Any of the 5 completions is incoherent, loops, or is entirely in the wrong language. → Reject.
3. **Instruction plumbing broken.** The "repeat exactly" prompt produces a paraphrase or ignores the format. → Reject.

**Promotion criterion:** all 5 completions are coherent, on-topic, and structurally correct. The model is *alive and talking sensibly*.

> *Why 5 prompts:* this is the minimum set that catches the three most common failure modes in open-weight releases (broken checkpoint, tokenizer mismatch, missing chat-template wiring) without spending more than a few hundred tokens of generation.

---

### Stage 2 — Fixed-Subset Calibration
**Budget: 30–60 minutes of GPU. 100–200 completions.**

What runs: a **versioned, frozen** evaluation battery. This is not a full benchmark; it is a stratified sample drawn from the benchmarks you actually care about:

| Sub-battery | Size | Source | What it catches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Factual recall | 40 | MMLU / TriviaQA sample | Catastrophic knowledge gaps |
| Arithmetic / reasoning | 30 | GSM8K subset | Basic reasoning broken |
| Instruction following | 30 | IFEval / custom | Formatting and constraint adherence |
| Code generation | 20 | HumanEval subset | Code sanity |
| Summarisation / extraction | 20 | Custom task prompts | Your actual workload shape |

All prompts, the sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, max tokens), and the scoring scripts are **pinned to a version** (see §4).

**Cheapest disqualifier:** a single sub-battery scoring below a **hard floor**. The floor is set per sub-battery and is *not* the adoption threshold — it is the "is this model broken" threshold.

Example floors (tune to your domain):

- Factual recall < 25% → reject
- Arithmetic < 20% → reject
- Instruction following < 30% → reject
- Any sub-battery < 15% → reject (regardless of which one)

**Promotion criterion:** every sub-battery clears its floor. The model is *competent enough to evaluate on your real tasks*.

> *Why floors, not a single aggregate:* a model that scores 80% on factual recall but 5% on instruction following is not "average" — it is broken for your use case. Per-battery floors prevent a strong sub-score from masking a catastrophic one.

---

### Stage 3 — Task-Relevant Evaluation
**Budget: 4–8 hours of GPU. 500–2 000 completions.**

What runs: a curated set of prompts drawn from **your actual workload**. This is the stage where the evaluation stops being generic and becomes specific to your product, research task, or pipeline.

Two components:

1. **Representative sample.** 300–500 prompts sampled from production logs, user tickets, or a manually curated task set. Scored with a mix of exact-match, LLM-as-judge (a fixed, pinned judge model), and human spot-checks (you or a colleague read 20–30 outputs).
2. **A/B against the current incumbent.** The same prompts are run against the model currently in production. You get a per-prompt win/loss/tie, not just a single aggregate number.

**Disqualifier:** the candidate does not meet the **adoption threshold** you pre-registered (see §5). Concretely:

- Win rate against incumbent < 50% (i.e., it is not better than what you already have), **or**
- Any critical task category (e.g., "safety refusal," "structured output") has a win rate < 40%.

**Promotion criterion:** the candidate beats the incumbent at or above the pre-registered threshold on the representative sample, with no critical category below its floor.

> *Why A/B instead of absolute scores:* absolute benchmark scores are noisy and not calibrated to your task. "Is it better than what I already run?" is the only question that matters at this stage.

---

### Stage 4 — Robustness and Edge Cases
**Budget: 8–16 hours of GPU. 1 000–3 000 completions.**

What runs: adversarial and edge-case probes. This is the stage that catches the failures that look fine on a representative sample:

- **Long-context degradation.** Prompts with 16k, 32k, 64k tokens of context. Does quality degrade gracefully or collapse?
- **Adversarial / jailbreak probes.** A fixed set of 50–100 known jailbreak and prompt-injection templates. (Not a safety certification — just "does it have the same failure modes as the incumbent?")
- **Distribution shift.** Prompts in domains the model was likely not trained on (e.g., your niche industry terminology).
- **Consistency.** Run 20 prompts 5× each with temperature > 0. Does the model produce wildly different answers, or is it stable?
- **Latency / throughput profile.** Measure tokens/sec on your hardware. If the model is 3× slower than the incumbent with no quality gain, that's a disqualifier.

**Disqualifier:** any of the following:

- Long-context quality drops below the Stage 2 floor at your required context length.
- > 20% of adversarial probes produce a safety failure that the incumbent does not.
- Consistency check shows > 30% of repeated prompts flip the answer.
- Throughput is < 50% of the incumbent's with no quality improvement.

**Promotion criterion:** all edge-case checks pass. The candidate is **adopted** (or queued for a human sign-off, see §5).

---

### Summary Table

| Stage | GPU Time | Completions | Question Answered | Disqualifier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 – Metadata | 0 | 0 | Is it even loadable / licensed / relevant? | License, arch, context, provenance |
| 1 – Smoke | ~15 min | 5 | Is it alive and talking? | Gibberish, broken plumbing |
| 2 – Calibration | ~45 min | 100–200 | Is it competent? | Any sub-battery below hard floor |
| 3 – Task-relevant | 4–8 h | 500–2 000 | Is it better than what I have? | Win rate below pre-registered threshold |
| 4 – Robustness | 8–16 h | 1 000–3 000 | Will it break in production? | Edge-case failure, latency regression |

Total worst-case GPU time for a single candidate: ~28 hours. Realistically, most candidates die at Stage 0 or 1, so the weekly budget covers 2–4 candidates that reach Stage 3 or 4.

---

## 3. What Evidence Promotes a Candidate

Promotion is **mechanical**, not judgmental. At each stage, the promotion decision is a function of the scores against pre-registered thresholds. There is no "I think it's good enough" step.

The evidence that promotes a candidate is:

1. **The raw scores** from that stage's evaluation battery, written to a results file.
2. **The pass/fail determination** computed by the scoring script, not by a human reading the numbers.
3. **A timestamped log entry** recording: model ID, revision, stage, scores, pass/fail, and the threshold that was applied.

A human may *inspect* the evidence (read a few completions, sanity-check a score), but the **gate decision is made by the script**. This is the single most important design choice for honesty (see §5).

---

## 4. Avoiding Re-Testing What Is Already Known

The biggest waste in a weekly process is re-running an evaluation that already ran last week on the same weights. Three mechanisms prevent this:

### 4.1 Content-Addressed Caching

Every evaluation result is keyed by a tuple:

```
cache_key = hash(
    model_id,          # e.g., "org/model-name"
    revision,          # git commit or HF revision hash of the weights
    eval_suite_version # version of the prompts + scoring script
)
```

Before any stage runs, the pipeline checks the cache. If the key exists, the stage is skipped and the cached result is used. This means:

- A model that was fully evaluated last week and has not been updated → **zero GPU time** this week.
- A model with a new revision (new weights) → full re-evaluation, because the key changed.
- An eval suite update (you added 10 prompts) → only the stages whose suite version changed re-run.

The cache is a local SQLite or JSON store. No infrastructure needed.

### 4.2 Suite Versioning

The evaluation batteries (the prompt sets, scoring scripts, sampling parameters) are versioned like code. Each version has a changelog. When you update a suite:

- Bump the version.
- Old results remain valid for the old version.
- New results are computed for the new version.
- You never silently change a prompt and expect the old score to still apply.

This prevents the subtle failure mode of "I tweaked a prompt last Tuesday, so the score from last week is no longer comparable, but I didn't notice."

### 4.3 Deduplication at Stage 0

Before anything is queued, the pipeline checks:

- Has this exact `(model_id, revision)` been evaluated before? → Skip entirely.
- Is this a known quantised variant (GGUF, AWQ, GPTQ) of a base model you already evaluated? → Evaluate only the quantisation-specific checks (Stage 1 smoke + latency), skip Stages 2–4 unless the base model was a close miss.
- Is this a LoRA / adapter for a base model you already have? → Evaluate the adapter on top of the cached base, not the full model.

---

## 5. Keeping the Process Honest When a Favourite Is Failing

This is the most important section. The failure mode is not technical; it is psychological. You have a model you *want* to adopt — it's from a team you admire, it's the "next big thing," it scored well on a viral benchmark tweet. It is failing your Stage 3 evaluation. What do you do?

The design answer is: **you do nothing. The script does.**

### 5.1 Pre-Register the Thresholds

Before the weekly evaluation cycle begins, the adoption thresholds (win rate, per-category floors, latency minimums) are written down in a config file and committed. They are set based on your requirements, not on any specific model.

You may update thresholds between weeks, but:

- The update is a code change with a commit message explaining why.
- The update applies to the *next* cycle, not the current one.
- You cannot change the threshold mid-evaluation and re-run.

This makes it structurally impossible to say "well, I'll lower the bar for this one."

### 5.2 The Gate Is a Script, Not a Person

The pass/fail decision at every stage is computed by the scoring script. The script reads the scores, compares them to the thresholds, and writes `PASS` or `FAIL` to the log. A human can read the log and the raw completions, but **the human does not set the pass/fail flag**.

If you want to override, you must:

1. Write a separate override file with a written justification.
2. The override is logged alongside the script's `FAIL` verdict, so the record shows both.
3. The override is reviewed by a second person (or by you, a week later, with fresh eyes).

This does not prevent override. It makes override **visible, logged, and accountable**.

### 5.3 The Graveyard Log

Every rejected model gets an entry in a permanent log:

```
2025-07-14 | org/some-model v2.1 | REJECTED at Stage 2
  Factual recall: 22% (floor: 25%)
  Arithmetic: 41% (floor: 20%) ✓
  Instruction following: 38% (floor: 30%) ✓
  Reason: factual recall below floor
```

This log is append-only. You cannot delete an entry. You cannot re-run a rejected model without a new revision or a new suite version (which changes the cache key and creates a new entry).

The graveyard log serves two purposes:

- **It makes re-testing a favourite expensive.** To re-evaluate a model you rejected last month, you must explain why the old rejection no longer applies. The log makes that explanation visible.
- **It calibrates your expectations.** After 20 weeks, you have a record of what actually passed and what didn't, and you can see whether your thresholds are too strict or too loose.

### 5.4 Separate Evaluation from Adoption

The person who runs the evaluation pipeline is not the person who makes the adoption decision (or, if it's the same person, the roles are separated in time). The evaluation produces a **report**: scores, pass/fail per stage, comparison to incumbent, edge-case findings. The adoption decision is a separate step that reads the report.

This separation means that the evaluation is not shaped by the desire to adopt. You are not tuning the eval to make the favourite pass. The eval runs the same way for every model, and the report is what it is.

### 5.5 The "One More Test" Rule

A common rationalisation: "The model failed instruction-following, but maybe it's a fluke. Let me run 50 more prompts on just that sub-battery."

The rule: **you may run one additional probe battery for a failed sub-battery, but the probe battery is pre-defined and versioned.** You cannot write new prompts on the fly to "see if it works better." The probe is a fixed set of 50 additional prompts from the same distribution, and the combined score (original + probe) is compared to the same threshold.

This allows for variance in a small sample without allowing for confirmation-seeking.

---

## 6. Operational Cadence

A weekly cycle looks like this:

| Day | Activity |
|---|---|
| **Monday** | Scan for new releases (HF trending, org announcements, arXiv). Run Stage 0 on all candidates. Queue survivors. |
| **Tuesday** | Run Stage 1 (smoke) on all queued candidates. Reject failures. |
| **Wednesday** | Run Stage 2 (calibration) on survivors. Reject failures. |
| **Thursday** | Run Stage 3 (task-relevant) on survivors. This is the expensive day. |
| **Friday** | Run Stage 4 (robustness) on the 1–2 survivors. Write the weekly report. Make adoption decisions. Update the graveyard log. |

If the GPU budget is exhausted before Friday, the remaining candidates are deferred to next week. The funnel does not skip stages to save time.

---

## 7. What This Document Does Not Cover

- **Model fine-tuning or distillation.** This is an evaluation pipeline, not a training pipeline. If a candidate is close but not quite good enough, the answer is "reject and fine-tune," not "lower the threshold."
- **Safety certification.** Stage 4's adversarial probes are a regression check, not a safety audit. If your deployment requires a formal safety evaluation, that is a separate, more expensive process.
- **Multi-model routing.** This document evaluates models one at a time. Deciding whether to route different tasks to different models is a downstream problem.
- **Continuous monitoring.** This is a weekly gate. Once a model is adopted, monitoring its quality in production is a separate system.

---

## 8. Implementation Notes

- **Orchestration:** a single Python script (or a small Makefile / Snakemake DAG) that runs stages in sequence, checks the cache before each stage, and writes results to SQLite. No cluster, no queue, no orchestration framework. One machine, one process.
- **Scoring:** exact-match and regex for structured tasks; a pinned judge model (a small, fixed model you run locally) for open-ended tasks. The judge model is versioned and never changed mid-cycle.
- **Prompts and suites:** stored in a git repo. The `eval_suite_version` in the cache key is the git commit hash of the suite repo.
- **The graveyard log:** a single Markdown or CSV file in the repo. Append-only by convention; enforced by a pre-commit hook that rejects deletions.
- **The report:** auto-generated from the SQLite results. One page per candidate. Stamped with the suite version and the model revision.
reasoning_head:
The user is asking for a design document for a "fail-fast funnel" — a staged evaluation pipeline for new open-weight model releases, run weekly on a single machine. They want:

1. Stages of the funnel
2. The cheapest disqualifying test at each stage
3. What evidence promotes a candidate to the next stage
4. How to avoid re-testing what is already known (caching/dedup)
5. How to keep the process honest when a favourite candidate is failing (bias mitigation)

This is a practical engineering/ML evaluation design doc. Let me think carefully about what makes this good.

Key constraints:
- One machine (so compute is the bottleneck — this drives the "cheapest test first" ordering)
- Weekly cadence (so there's a fixed budget per week, and you need to handle multiple releases)
- Open-weight models (so you can download weights, run inference, and inspect them)
- Fail-fast (cheapest disqualifier first, escalate cost only for survivors)

Let me think about realistic stages for evaluating an open-weight model:

Stage 0: Metadata triage (free/near-free)
- Check the model card, architecture, parameter count, context window, license
- Disqualifier: license incompatible with your use, architecture you can't load, context window too small
- Cost: reading a README, checking a config file

Stage 1: Loadability / smoke test (minutes)
- Can you actually load the weights? Does it produce coherent output on 3-5 trivial prompts?
- Disqualifier: broken weights, tokenizer mismatch, OOM on your machine, gibberish output
- Cost: a few minutes of GPU time, maybe 5-10 prompts

Stage 2: Calibration / sanity checks (tens of minutes)
- Run a small fixed battery of known-answer questions (MMLU-lite subset, GSM8K subset, etc.)
- Disqualifier: score below a hard floor (e.g., <30% on a 50-question subset)
- Cost: maybe 50-100 completions

Stage 3: Task-relevant evaluation (hours)
- Run your actual use-case benchmarks, a curated set of prompts representative of your workload
- Disqualifier: doesn't meet the threshold for your specific task
- Cost: hundreds to low thousands of completions

Stage 4: Robustness / edge cases (hours to a day)
- Adversarial prompts, long-context behavior, instruction-following edge cases, safety
- Disqualifier: catastrophic failure modes
- Cost: more completions, possibly with varied sampling

Stage 5: Full evaluation / deployment readiness (days)
- Full benchmark suite, A/B against current production model, latency profiling
- Promotion: this is where you actually decide to adopt

Now for the "avoid re-testing" part:
- Hash the model weights (or at least the checkpoint URL + revision)
- Cache results keyed by (model_id, revision, eval_suite_version, prompt_hash)
- If a model was tested last week and only a minor revision came out, skip stages that already passed
- Version your eval suites so you know when re-testing is actually needed

For the "honesty with favourites" part:

# Revenue Forecasting: Online vs. Brick-and-Mortar

## The Core Shared Formula

Both models ultimately boil down to:

**Revenue = Customers × Conversion Rate × Average Order Value (AOV)**

The differences live in *how* each variable behaves, what data you have, and what external forces move them.

---

## Online Business

**Key drivers to model:**
- **Traffic volume** (sessions, visitors) — often the leading indicator. You forecast traffic first, then apply conversion.
- **Conversion rate** — typically 1–3%. Highly sensitive to UX, page speed, product page quality, and review counts.
- **AOV and basket size** — influenced by cross-sell/upsell mechanics, bundle offers, and shipping-threshold nudges.
- **Customer acquisition channels** — paid ads (PPC, social), SEO, email, affiliates. Each channel has its own CAC and conversion curve, so you often forecast *by channel* and sum.
- **Retention / repeat purchase rate** — subscription or repeat-buyer cohorts. LTV curves matter a lot.

**Data advantages:**
- You get granular, real-time data: clickstreams, cart abandonment rates, cohort retention, email open/click rates, ad-level ROAS.
- You can run controlled experiments (A/B tests) to validate assumptions before scaling spend.
- Seasonality is visible in clean time-series data (Google Trends, your own analytics).

**Unique variables:**
- Ad platform algorithm changes (e.g., Meta's delivery shifts) can swing CAC overnight.
- SEO ranking volatility.
- Platform dependency (Amazon, Shopify, App Store) — one policy change can wipe out a revenue stream.
- Almost no geographic constraint, so "capacity" is usually server/fulfillment, not shelf space.

**Typical method:** Channel-by-channel funnel model. Forecast traffic per channel → apply historical conversion → apply AOV → add retention/repeat revenue. Often supplemented with cohort-based LTV models.

---

## Brick-and-Mortar Retailer

**Key drivers to model:**
- **Foot traffic** — the analog of "sessions." Driven by location, local demographics, mall/strip-center performance, and local events.
- **Conversion rate** — in-store conversion is usually 20–40% (much higher than online), but you rarely have clean per-visitor data. You often estimate it from POS transactions ÷ door counters.
- **AOV / basket size** — influenced by store layout, promotions, and whether customers browse the full store vs. grab one item.
- **Store count and square footage** — your "capacity" is physical. Adding a store is a discrete, lumpy revenue step.
- **Local competition and trade-area shifts** — a new competitor opening two blocks away, or a mall losing an anchor tenant, directly hits revenue.

**Data challenges:**
- You often lack per-visitor tracking (unless you have door counters or loyalty-card data).
- Attribution is murkier: did a customer buy because of the Instagram ad, the in-store display, or the radio spot?
- Seasonality is more location-specific (a ski-town shop vs. a beach town).

**Unique variables:**
- **Real estate costs and lease terms** — rent escalations, CAM charges, and lease expirations affect net revenue feasibility even if gross revenue is flat.
- **Inventory and shelf-space constraints** — you can't just "add more product pages." Stockouts and markdowns directly hit revenue.
- **Labor capacity** — understaffing during a peak weekend caps transactions.
- **Local economic indicators** — median household income in the trade area, local employment trends, construction activity.
- **Weather and local events** — a rainy Saturday or a city festival matters far more than it does for an online store.

**Typical method:** Store-level model. Forecast per-store revenue using historical sales by product category, adjust for local seasonality, trade-area trends, and planned promotions. Then aggregate across locations. Often grounded in comparable-store analysis ("comps").

---

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Dimension | Online | Brick-and-Mortar |
|---|---|---|
| Primary leading indicator | Digital traffic / ad spend | Foot traffic / local demand |
| Conversion rate | ~1–3% | ~20–40% |
| Geographic scope | National/global | Local trade area |
| Capacity constraint | Fulfillment, servers | Shelf space, labor, square footage |
| Data granularity | Very high (per click, per session) | Moderate (POS + door counts) |
| Biggest volatility source | Ad platform / SEO changes | Local competition, weather, lease events |
| Scaling mechanism | Add channels, increase ad spend | Open new stores (lumpy, capital-intensive) |
| Forecasting granularity | Often by channel + cohort | Often by store + product category |
| Seasonality | Global patterns (Prime Day, holidays) | Local + global patterns |

---

## Practical Tips for Both

1. **Build a bottom-up model, not just a top-down line.** "Last year's revenue × 10% growth" misses the *why*. Decompose into the funnel.
2. **Scenario-plan.** Build optimistic / base / pessimistic cases. Online businesses swing harder on ad-cost shocks; physical stores swing harder on local events.
3. **Track leading indicators weekly**, not just monthly revenue. Online: CAC, conversion, email list growth. Physical: foot traffic, sell-through rate, inventory turns.
4. **Watch for structural breaks.** A new product line, a store opening, or a shift from paid to organic traffic changes the model's assumptions. Re-baseline after these events.
5. **Hybrid is the norm now.** Most retailers have both. Forecast each channel separately, then reconcile so you're not double-counting a customer who browsed online and bought in-store (or vice versa).

# Local Model-Serving Router — Architecture

## Topology

```
                        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                        │              ROUTER (single process)         │
                        │                                             │
  Interactive client ──►│  Admission    Scheduler    Swap Engine      │
  (HTTP/SSE, 1 conn)    │  Control ──►  (priority  ──►  (load/unload)│
                        │  (auth,      queue)         ──►  Model      │
  Benchmark runner ────►│   rate-limit,    │              Registry    │
  (gRPC batch, N jobs)  │   session TTL)   │              (1 slot)    │
                        │                 ▼                          │
                        │           Memory Ledger ◄── CUDA            │
                        │           (VRAM budget)      driver        │
                        │                 │                          │
                        └─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘
                                          ▼
                                    ┌──────────────┐
                                    │  GPU (1 slot)│
                                    │  model + KV  │
                                    └──────────────┘
```

One router process, one GPU, one model resident at a time. The router is the only thing that touches the model lifecycle. Clients never talk to the inference backend directly.

---

## 1. Admission Control

Two queues, one priority rule:

| Class | Queue | Admission rule |
|---|---|---|
| Interactive | `iq` (FIFO, max depth 1) | Always admitted. If the requested model ≠ resident model, the request enters a **swap-wait** state and the client receives a `202` with an ETA header, not a silent hang. |
| Benchmark | `bq` (FIFO, max depth 32) | Admitted only when the resident model matches *and* no interactive request is pending. Otherwise it parks. |

The interactive queue is depth-1 by design. A human generates one turn at a time; anything deeper is a bug or a script masquerading as a user. Reject the second concurrent interactive request with `429` and a reason.

Benchmark jobs declare their model, batch size, and expected duration at submission. The router uses that metadata for swap scheduling (below).

---

## 2. Model Registry and the Single Slot

The registry is a small in-memory table (persisted to a JSON file so restarts don't lose warm-model hints):

```
{
  "slot": {
    "model_id": "llama-3-70b-instruct",
    "loaded_at": 1717000000,
    "last_used_at": 1717000042,
    "kv_cache_bytes": 838860800,
    "weights_bytes": 140000000000
  },
  "candidates": {
    "llama-3-70b-instruct": { "load_time_s": 52, "weights_bytes": 140e9 },
    "mistral-7b":          { "load_time_s": 4,  "weights_bytes": 13e9 }
  }
}
```

`load_time_s` is measured on first load and updated on every subsequent load (cold page cache vs warm). The swap engine uses it to compute ETAs.

The slot is guarded by a single mutex. Only the swap engine acquires it. Generation requests acquire a lighter "model-in-use" lease so the swap engine can't yank the model out from under a running decode step.

---

## 3. Swap Policy

This is the part that makes or breaks the system. The policy is a **cost-aware preempt-or-wait** decision, evaluated when an interactive request arrives and the resident model doesn't match.

```
on interactive_request(model M):
    if resident == M:
        serve immediately
        return

    resident = current model
    bench_remaining = bq.front().expected_remaining_s   # 0 if bq empty

    swap_cost = registry[M].load_time_s + bench_loss(bench)

    if bench_remaining < SWAP_THRESHOLD (≈ 90 s):
        # benchmark is close to done; let it finish, then swap
        park request, ETA = bench_remaining + swap_cost
    elif bench_remaining > BENCH_GRACE (≈ 300 s) and bench_progress > 0.8:
        # benchmark is 80%+ done; finish it
        park request, ETA = bench_remaining + swap_cost
    else:
        # preempt now
        cancel bench batch (checkpoint if supported)
        swap to M
        serve
```

Key parameters and why:

- **Sticky dwell**: after serving an interactive turn, the model stays resident for `STICKY_S = 120 s`. Follow-up turns (which are the common case) hit a warm model. The benchmark queue is blocked during this window.
- **Swap cooldown**: minimum `COOLDOWN_S = 60 s` between any two swaps. Prevents thrash when a user switches models rapidly.
- **Benchmark checkpointing**: if the benchmark framework supports it (e.g., it can save completed samples to disk), the swap engine signals a graceful stop at the next sample boundary rather than killing mid-generation. If it doesn't, the swap engine kills the process and the benchmark runner re-submits from its last checkpoint.

The policy is deliberately simple. A learned scheduler is the wrong tool for one machine with two traffic classes; a decision tree with three branches is debuggable.

---

## 4. Session Caching

Two layers, because "session cache" means different things at different timescales:

**KV cache (in-VRAM, per active sequence).**
The inference backend (llama.cpp, vLLM, whatever) manages this. The router's only concern is the memory ledger (below). When the user stops a generation, the router tells the backend to release the KV block for that sequence immediately, not at turn end. This reclaims VRAM for the next turn or a swap.

**Model residency TTL (the real "session cache").**
With one model slot, the only way to keep a session fast is to keep its model loaded. The router tracks `last_used_at` per model. The swap engine treats a model with `last_used_at` within `STICKY_S` as "hot" and resists evicting it for a benchmark job. A benchmark job that wants a *different* model must wait for the sticky window to expire or the interactive user to go idle for `IDLE_EVICT_S = 300 s`.

**CPU-side prompt cache (optional, cheap).**
If the interactive client sends long system prompts repeatedly, cache the tokenized prompt bytes in RAM. Re-tokenization is fast enough that this is a minor optimization, but it avoids a 200 ms hiccup on model swap.

---

## 5. Request Cancellation

Three cancellation sources, each with different semantics:

| Source | Scope | Action |
|---|---|---|
| User hits Stop | One generation | Backend aborts decode loop, releases KV block. Router marks sequence done. Model stays resident. |
| User closes tab / disconnects | One session | Same as above, plus start the `IDLE_EVICT_S` countdown. |
| Swap engine preempts benchmark | Entire benchmark batch | Signal SIGTERM to benchmark process. Wait `GRACE_S = 10 s`. SIGKILL if still alive. Acquire slot mutex. Unload. Load new model. |

The critical invariant: **cancellation must be synchronous with respect to the slot mutex.** The swap engine must not begin unloading until the backend confirms all in-flight sequences are drained and KV is freed. Otherwise you get a CUDA context that's half-torn-down and the next load fails with a cryptic driver error.

Implementation: the backend exposes a `drain(timeout)` call. The swap engine calls it, blocks, and only proceeds on success or timeout. On timeout, it escalates to a full backend process restart (kill + relaunch), which is the nuclear option but the only reliable way to recover a wedged CUDA context.

---

## 6. Memory Accounting

A **Memory Ledger** object in the router tracks VRAM in bytes, not percentages. The budget is `TOTAL_VRAM` (queried once at startup via `nvidia-smi` / `cudaDeviceGetProperties`).

```
TOTAL_VRAM
  ├── cuda_context        (~800 MB, fixed, measured once)
  ├── model_weights       (from registry, known before load)
  ├── kv_cache_allocated  (backend reports after each batch)
  ├── activations_peak    (backend reports, high-water mark per sequence)
  └── free               (computed; must stay > MIN_FREE)
```

Rules:

- **Pre-load check**: before loading model M, the ledger verifies `free ≥ weights(M) + MIN_KV + MIN_FREE`. `MIN_KV` is the KV for one interactive sequence at the model's max context (e.g., 4096 tokens × 2 × 8 bytes × n_layers). `MIN_FREE` is a 2 GB safety margin for CUDA allocations and fragmentation. If the check fails, the swap is refused and the request is rejected with a clear error.

- **Post-load verification**: after the backend reports the model is loaded, the ledger reads actual VRAM usage. If it exceeds the predicted budget by more than 10%, log a warning (the model's real memory footprint differs from the config estimate — this happens with some quantization formats).

- **KV growth guard**: the backend reports `kv_cache_allocated` after every generation step. If it approaches `free - MIN_FREE`, the router truncates the context (drops oldest KV blocks) rather than letting the backend OOM. This is the interactive equivalent of a context-window limit, enforced by the router rather than the backend.

- **Fragmentation tracking**: log `free` after every swap. If `free` after unload is less than `free` before load (i.e., the GPU didn't give memory back), increment a fragmentation counter. After 3 consecutive swaps with growing fragmentation, trigger a backend restart to reclaim.

---

## 7. Failure Modes to Instrument First

Ordered by "how much pain this causes and how hard it is to debug without telemetry":

### 7.1 OOM during model load
**What happens**: The backend starts loading a 140 GB model into 80 GB of VRAM. It allocates 40 GB, hits the wall, and either crashes or (worse) leaves a half-loaded model that holds VRAM but can't serve.
**Instrument**: The pre-load check in §6 catches the obvious case. For the subtle case (model loads but KV allocation fails on first request), instrument the backend's first-token latency and VRAM delta. If `free < 0` after load, treat as a failed load: unload, log, reject.
**Alert**: any OOM event. This is a config error or a model that's too big for the hardware.

### 7.2 Swap thrash
**What happens**: User switches between two models every 40 seconds. The swap engine loads/unloads in a loop. The machine is 100% busy loading models and serves nothing.
**Instrument**: Count swaps in a sliding 10-minute window. If `swaps > 5`, the cooldown should have prevented this. If it didn't, the cooldown timer is broken or the user is hammering the API. Log the model sequence. Alert at `swaps > 8`.
**Mitigation**: The cooldown in §3 is the primary defense. The alert is the backstop.

### 7.3 Interactive latency regression
**What happens**: A benchmark job that's "supposed to be background" is actually consuming all the compute, and interactive requests get 12-second time-to-first-token instead of 1.5 seconds.
**Instrument**: Track `time_to_first_token` and `tokens_per_second` per request, tagged with the traffic class. Alert if interactive p99 TTFT > 5 s over a 5-minute window. This is the single most important metric for the daily-driver experience.
**Mitigation**: The admission control in §1 blocks benchmark admission when interactive traffic is active. If TTFT still degrades, the benchmark is running *on the same model* as the interactive user and stealing compute. The router should throttle benchmark batch size to leave headroom (e.g., cap benchmark concurrent sequences at 1 when an interactive session is active).

### 7.4 Zombie GPU memory after crash
**What happens**: The backend process segfaults. The OS reclaims the process but the CUDA context (and its VRAM) is not released until the GPU driver reclaims it, which can take 30+ seconds or never happen if the driver is wedged.
**Instrument**: After any backend process exit (expected or not), poll `nvidia-smi` for 30 seconds. If the GPU's memory usage doesn't drop to the baseline (~800 MB context), escalate: kill any orphaned child processes, then `nvidia-smi --gpu-reset` (if available), then alert a human.
**This is the failure mode that turns a 5-second hiccup into a "I have to reboot the machine" event.**

### 7.5 Benchmark starvation
**What happens**: The interactive user is active 16 hours a day. The benchmark job has been parked for 22 hours. It never runs.
**Instrument**: Track `bq.front().age`. Alert at 1 hour. The swap policy in §3 should eventually let it run during the sticky window, but if the user is genuinely active 24/7, the benchmark will never get a slot. This is a policy problem, not a code bug — the alert tells the user their benchmark is stuck.
**Mitigation**: The benchmark runner should declare a `deadline`. If it misses the deadline, the router cancels it and reports the reason.

### 7.6 Stale session after model swap
**What happens**: User has a 50-turn conversation with model A. The model gets evicted for a benchmark. User sends turn 51. The router loads model A, but the KV cache is gone, so the model has no memory of turns 1–50. It responds as if the conversation just started.
**Instrument**: Track `session_turn_count` and `kv_cache_present`. If a request arrives with `turn_count > 1` and `kv_cache_present == false`, log a `session_amnesia` event. This is expected behavior, but the client should be told: the router returns a `session_reset: true` flag so the client can re-inject the conversation history.
**Mitigation**: The sticky dwell in §4 minimizes this. For long sessions, the client-side prompt cache (§4) re-injects history.

---

## 8. Process Model

The router is a single long-running process (Rust or Go; the scheduler and ledger need to be fast and the memory model simple). The inference backend is a **child process** that the router spawns and can kill. This is the single most important architectural decision:

- The backend owns the CUDA context. Killing the process is the only reliable way to reclaim a wedged context.
- The router communicates with the backend over a local Unix socket with a simple JSON-RPC protocol: `load(model)`, `unload()`, `generate(prompt, max_tokens, stream)`, `drain(timeout)`, `report_memory()`.
- The backend is stateless across restarts. All session state lives in the router.

If the backend dies, the router detects it (socket EOF or heartbeat timeout at 5 s), marks the slot empty, and the next request triggers a fresh spawn + load. The user sees a gap, not a crash.

---

## 9. What I Would Not Do

- **No GPU sharing / MPS / MIG.** With one model slot, there's nothing to share. MPS adds a failure mode (one process's OOM kills the other) for zero benefit.
- **No model quantization switching at runtime.** If the user wants a smaller model, they request it by name and the router swaps. The router doesn't decide to quantize the loaded model to fit.
- **No learned scheduler.** Three traffic classes on one machine doesn't need reinforcement learning. A decision tree with logged decisions is debuggable in an afternoon. A learned policy is a black box you debug by turning it off.
- **No multi-GPU.** The constraint is one machine, one model. If you have two GPUs, that's a different architecture (two slots, round-robin). Don't solve that problem here.

# KV-Cache Compression & Eviction for Long-Context Inference

## 1. Sliding-Window / Local Attention

**Mechanism.** Each token attends only to the last *W* positions (e.g. 4 096). The KV cache is a fixed-size ring buffer; old entries are overwritten. Mistral-7B and Longformer use this natively.

**Quality cost.** Hard loss of anything beyond *W*. A reference to a type defined 30 k tokens earlier is simply invisible. The degradation is *positional*: it hits the oldest content first, regardless of whether it was important.

**Suits.** Local reasoning, single-file code completion, chat where the conversation is self-contained. Unsuitable whenever the answer depends on a distant anchor (an import at the top of a 200 k-token file).

---

## 2. Attention Sinks + Window (StreamingLLM)

**Mechanism.** Keep the first *k* tokens (typically 4) as "sinks" that absorb the diffuse attention mass every head would otherwise spread over early positions, plus a sliding window of the most recent *W* tokens.

**Quality cost.** Slightly better than pure SWA for perplexity and streaming continuation, because the sinks prevent the model from "forgetting" that a sequence started. But it still cannot *recall* a specific fact from the middle of the stream.

**Suits.** Infinite streaming (live logs, terminal output). Not a general-purpose long-context solution.

---

## 3. Heavy-Hitter Oracle / H2O

**Mechanism.** Maintain a running sum of attention mass received by each token across all heads and layers. Evict the tokens with the lowest cumulative score, keeping a fixed top-*K*. Selection is O(N) per step but amortised.

**Quality cost.** Two failure modes:
- *Deferred importance*: a token that is only relevant after 50 k tokens of context (e.g. a type alias used once near the end) may have near-zero cumulative attention and gets evicted before it matters.
- *Uniform-distribution tasks*: summarisation or "find every TODO" need broad recall; heavy-hitter selection concentrates on a few hot tokens and blurs the rest.

**Suits.** General long-context QA and multi-turn dialogue where attention is naturally concentrated. A good default eviction policy when you must cap cache size.

---

## 4. SnapKV / Per-Head Clustering

**Mechanism.** At a selection checkpoint (usually near the end of the prompt), run one forward pass over a short "observation window" (last ~64 tokens). For *each attention head*, rank all prior KV pairs by the attention they received from that window and keep the top-*k*. Different heads keep different tokens.

**Quality cost.** One-time O(N·H·W_obs) cost at selection. If the observation window doesn't exercise the right tokens, you evict them permanently. Quality on single-turn extraction (summarise this document, answer this question) is strong; on iterative multi-turn tasks the static selection can go stale.

**Suits.** Single-turn, prompt-then-answer workloads: document QA, summarisation, one-shot code review. Less suited to agentic loops where the "question" changes every turn.

---

## 5. KV-Cache Quantisation

**Mechanism.** Store K and V tensors in INT8 or INT4 instead of FP16/BF16. No tokens are evicted; every token is kept but at lower precision. vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and llama.cpp all support this.

**Quality cost.** INT8: typically < 1 % degradation on most benchmarks. INT4: 2–5 %, more visible on tasks that need to distinguish similar tokens (code identifiers, error messages). Combines multiplicatively with eviction methods.

**Suits.** Universal. The cheapest first move: halve or quarter memory with negligible quality loss, then layer an eviction policy on top.

---

## 6. Token Merging / Learned Summarisation (Gisting, ICAE)

**Mechanism.** A small compression network maps *N* tokens → *M* tokens (M ≪ N) in the KV space, trained with a reconstruction or task objective. The compressed "gist" tokens replace the originals in the cache.

**Quality cost.** Inherently lossy. At 10:1 ratio you retain gist-level semantics but lose verbatim detail—exact identifiers, line numbers, stack-trace text. Quality degrades smoothly with ratio, unlike hard eviction which has a cliff.

**Suits.** Pre-compressing *known, stable* context: system prompts, API documentation, style guides. Not ideal for content the agent must quote or match exactly.

---

## 7. Head- / Layer-Aware Differential Budgets

**Mechanism.** Empirical studies (e.g. "The Power of Positional Attention") show that a small set of "positional" heads need every token, while "content" heads attend to a sparse subset. Allocate a large budget to positional heads and a small one to content heads, or skip KV storage entirely for heads that are near-identity.

**Quality cost.** Reduces the "one-size-fits-all" cliff of global eviction. Residual cost is concentrated in the content heads, which is usually where you can afford it.

**Suits.** Any workload where you can afford a per-head bookkeeping overhead. Pairs well with H2O or SnapKV: apply the eviction policy only to content heads.

---

## 8. External Retrieval / Agentic Memory

**Mechanism.** Keep only a small working set in the KV cache. Store compressed embeddings or summaries of the rest in an external index (vector DB, paged store). At each step, retrieve the top-*r* relevant chunks and prepend them.

**Quality cost.** Retrieval miss = information loss, and it's *stochastic*—the same query can miss on one run and hit on another. Adds retrieval latency (tens of ms) per step.

**Suits.** RAG pipelines, agentic workflows with many turns, anything where the "relevant subset" shifts between steps. The natural fit for a coding agent that hops between files.

---

## Quick Comparison

| Approach | Cache size | Quality risk | Multi-turn? | Implementation cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sliding window | O(W) | High (positional) | Yes | Trivial |
| Sinks + window | O(W+k) | High (positional) | Yes | Trivial |
| H2O | O(K) | Medium (deferred importance) | Yes | Low |
| SnapKV | O(H·k) | Medium (stale selection) | No (single-turn) | Low |
| Quantisation | O(N) × bits | Low | Yes | Trivial |
| Gisting | O(M) | Medium–High (lossy) | Yes | High (training) |
| Head-aware budgets | O(Σ per-head) | Low–Medium | Yes | Medium |
| External retrieval | O(r) working | Medium (retrieval miss) | Yes | High (infra) |

---

## Recommendation: Coding Agent That Reads Whole Repositories

The workload has a distinctive shape:

- **Structured, hierarchical context.** Files → classes → functions. Attention is strongly local within a function but has a few long-range spikes (imports, type references, call sites).
- **Shifting relevance.** The agent explores file A, then jumps to file B. The "hot" tokens change every turn, so a one-shot SnapKV selection goes stale quickly.
- **Exact-recall demands.** The agent must reproduce identifiers, signatures, and error strings verbatim—gist compression will mangle these.
- **Huge but sparse.** A 200 k-token repo dump is mostly boilerplate; the information density is low and concentrated.

A layered strategy works best:

1. **Quantise the full cache to INT8** (or INT4 for K only). This is the floor: you keep every token, just at half or quarter precision. Cost is near-zero quality loss and it buys 2–4× headroom.

2. **Head-aware eviction on top.** Keep all tokens in the ~10–20 % of heads that are positional/structural. For the remaining content heads, run a lightweight H2O-style cumulative-attention tracker and evict the bottom 50–70 % of tokens. This preserves the long-range spikes (imports, type refs) while shedding boilerplate. Because it's cumulative and updated every step, it adapts to the agent's shifting focus—unlike SnapKV's one-shot selection.

3. **Structural-token pinning.** Before eviction, mark tokens that correspond to file headers, `import`/`#include` lines, class and function signatures, and type declarations. These are cheap to identify (regex or tree-sitter) and are the tokens the agent most needs to recall. Exempt them from eviction.

4. **Sliding window for the active file.** The file the agent is currently editing or reading should always be in full, unevicted form in the most recent *W* positions. This is the working set.

5. **External retrieval as a safety net.** Index the full repo into a vector store (or a lightweight BM25 index over code tokens). When the agent references a symbol not in the current cache, retrieve the relevant chunk and prepend it. This catches the deferred-importance failure mode of H2O without keeping everything resident.

6. **Avoid gisting for code.** The lossy compression of gisting/ICAE is too risky when the agent must emit exact identifiers. Reserve it, if at all, for compressing stable system-prompt or documentation context.

The net effect: you keep roughly 30–50 % of the raw tokens in the KV cache (after quantisation + head-aware eviction), you always have the active file intact, and you have a retrieval fallback for the rest. This gives you the recall of a full-context model at roughly a quarter of the memory cost, with the adaptivity a static selection method can't provide in a multi-turn agentic loop.

# Dataset Type Classification: Master Data vs. Transactional

## Core Hypothesis

Master data is **reference-centric, slowly changing, and highly referenced**. Transactional data is **event-centric, append-heavy, and references master data**. The algorithm should score a dataset across several orthogonal dimensions and combine them.

---

## 1. Structural / Schema Analysis

| Signal | Calculation | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Column-type ratio** | `ratio_numeric = count(numeric/decimal cols) / total_cols` | High → transactional (measures: qty, amount, price). Low → master (descriptive: name, address, code). |
| **Timestamp role** | Detect columns with `TIMESTAMP / DATE` type. Compute `distinct(ts) / row_count`. | ≈ 1.0 → event time (transactional). << 1.0 → effective/valid-from date (master). |
| **FK fan-in** | Count of other tables whose FK points **into** this table. | High fan-in → master (many orders reference one customer). Low → transactional. |
| **FK fan-out** | Count of FK columns **in** this table pointing to other tables. | High fan-out → transactional (an order references customer, product, warehouse). |
| **Column count** | Simple count. | Master tables tend to have fewer, richer columns; transactional tables often have more measure/status columns. |

**Score contribution:** weighted sum, e.g.
```
S_schema = w1*(1 - ratio_numeric) + w2*(1 - ts_uniqueness) 
         + w3*(fan_in / max_fan_in) - w4*(fan_out / max_fan_out)
```

---

## 2. Temporal / Change-Log Analysis

This is the strongest signal if you have CDC / audit logs.

- **Insert-to-Update ratio**
  ```
  IUR = INSERTS / (INSERTS + UPDATES)
  ```
  - Transactional: IUR → 1.0 (almost pure append).
  - Master: IUR ≈ 0.5 or lower (rows get corrected, re-classified, re-addressed).

- **Growth rate**
  ```
  g = (rows(t2) - rows(t1)) / (t2 - t1)   # rows per day
  ```
  Normalise by table size: `g / avg_row_count`. Transactional tables grow fast relative to their base; master tables grow slowly.

- **Timestamp recency skew**
  ```
  skew = 1 - (distinct_ts_in_recent_30d / distinct_ts_overall)
  ```
  Transactional: high skew (most activity is recent). Master: low skew (records span years evenly).

- **Update recency**
  ```
  % of rows updated in last 90 days
  ```
  Master: can be moderate-to-high (a customer's address changes). Transactional: very low (an order from 2019 isn't touched).

---

## 3. Cardinality & Content Statistics

- **Key entropy**
  ```
  H(key) = -Σ p(v) log₂ p(v)    over the primary/surrogate key values
  ```
  Both types have high key entropy, but the *distribution of non-key columns* differs.

- **Categorical vs. measure columns**
  For each column compute `distinct / row_count` (NDV ratio).
  ```
  categorical_cols = columns where NDV_ratio < 0.05   (e.g., status, type, country)
  measure_cols     = columns where NDV_ratio > 0.5 AND type is numeric
  S_content = categorical_cols / total_cols
  ```
  High `S_content` → master. High `measure_cols` → transactional.

- **Value distribution shape**
  - Master: attributes are often **sparse / skewed** (most customers are in 2–3 countries).
  - Transactional: measures are often **continuous / near-uniform** (amounts, quantities).
  Use **Shannon entropy per column** or **coefficient of variation (σ/μ)** as a quick discriminator.

---

## 4. Referential & Relationship Graph

Build a directed graph of FK relationships across the schema.

- **In-degree** (how many tables reference this one) → master indicator.
- **Out-degree** (how many tables this one references) → transactional indicator.
- **Position in the graph**: master tables sit at the "hub" / top of the hierarchy; transactional tables are leaves or mid-level.

You can run a simple **PageRank** or **betweenness centrality** on the FK graph; high centrality → master.

---

## 5. Volume & Lifecycle Heuristics

| Metric | Master | Transactional |
|---|---|---|
| Row count | 10³ – 10⁶ (bounded) | 10⁶ – 10⁹+ (unbounded) |
| Avg. record age | years | hours – months |
| Delete rate | ~0 (soft-delete / archive) | ~0 (append-only) or batch purge |
| Rows per FK parent | 1 (or few) | many (orders per customer) |

```
S_volume = log10(row_count) / log10(max_row_count_in_schema)
S_age    = avg(record_age) / max(record_age)
```

---

## 6. Combining into a Final Score

```
Score = Σ  wᵢ · Sᵢ        (each Sᵢ normalised to [0, 1])

  S₁  schema
  S₂  temporal / change-log
  S₃  content statistics
  S₄  graph centrality
  S₅  volume / lifecycle

Classification:
  Score > θ  →  MASTER
  Score ≤ θ  →  TRANSACTIONAL
```

- Weights `wᵢ` can start equal and be **tuned with labelled examples** (a small set of ~50–100 tables you manually tag) using logistic regression or a simple gradient-descent fit.
- Threshold `θ` ≈ 0.5 initially; adjust with precision/recall on the labelled set.

---

## 7. Practical Caveats & Edge Cases

- **Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)**: SCD2 tables look hybrid (master keys + event timestamps). Add a feature: `ratio of duplicate business keys` → if > 1, it's SCD2, classify as master but flag it.
- **Reference / lookup tables** (country codes, currency): tiny, static → master, but with near-zero change volume. The volume heuristic alone would misclassify; the fan-in heuristic saves you.
- **Log / audit tables**: append-only, high volume, but no FK fan-out. Treat as transactional.
- **Hybrid tables** (e.g., a "customer" table that also stores the latest order amount): the algorithm will give a mid-range score; consider a **three-class** output (master / transactional / hybrid) or a confidence interval.

---

## TL;DR Algorithm Sketch

```python
def classify(table):
    s_schema  = schema_features(table)      # col types, ts role, FK in/out
    s_temporal= change_log_features(table)  # IUR, growth rate, recency skew
    s_content = content_stats(table)        # NDV ratios, entropy per col
    s_graph   = fk_graph_centrality(table)  # in-degree, PageRank
    s_volume  = volume_lifecycle(table)     # row count, avg age

    score = w @ [s_schema, s_temporal, s_content, s_graph, s_volume]
    return "MASTER" if score > theta else "TRANSACTIONAL", score
```

The **change-log / temporal signals** (insert-vs-update ratio, growth rate, recency skew) tend to carry the most discriminative power in practice, so I'd weight them highest once you have the data. Schema and graph features are your fallback when audit logs are unavailable.

# MoE vs. Dense Transformers for Local, Memory-Constrained Inference

## The core structural difference

A dense transformer reads **every** parameter on every token. A mixture-of-experts model has a large pool of feed-forward experts but routes each token to only *k* of them (typically 2 out of 8). This creates a split between **total parameters** (everything you must store) and **active parameters** (what you actually compute with per token). That split is the source of every tradeoff below.

---

## Memory

This is where MoE is most often misunderstood.

- **Dense:** memory footprint ≈ model size. A 13B model at Q4_K_M is roughly 8 GB. You load it once, it fits, you're done.
- **MoE:** you must keep **all** experts resident to avoid per-token disk I/O. Mixtral 8×7B has ~129 B total parameters (~13 B active). At Q4_K_M that's roughly **65–70 GB** of weights. The "13 B active" number tells you the compute cost per token, not the memory cost.

The escape hatch is **expert offloading**: keep experts on NVMe and stream the two active experts into RAM per token. In practice this adds 10–100 ms of I/O latency per token (or worse on consumer SSDs), causes cache thrashing because routing is token-dependent, and makes latency highly variable. For an interactive assistant that needs to feel responsive, this is a non-starter.

**Bottom line:** for a fixed memory budget, a dense model gives you more active parameters per byte. A 13B dense model at Q4 fits in 8 GB; the equivalent "13B active" MoE model needs 65 GB to be fully resident.

## Latency

- **Dense:** latency per token is dominated by memory bandwidth (moving all weights through the compute unit). It is **predictable and uniform** across tokens.
- **MoE (fully resident):** fewer active parameters means less data to move per token, so *if it fits in memory*, per-token latency can be lower than a dense model of the same total size. Routing adds a small overhead (a few microseconds). However, expert selection varies token-to-token, so the working set of touched memory is less cache-friendly, adding variance.
- **MoE (partially resident / offloaded):** latency spikes whenever a needed expert isn't in the hot cache. You get a bimodal distribution—fast when experts are cached, painful stalls when they aren't.

For an interactive assistant where the user is watching tokens stream in, **variance is as bad as mean latency**. Dense models win on latency predictability.

## Quantization behaviour

- **Dense models** have a well-trodden quantization path. Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0 are extensively benchmarked; quality degradation is gradual and predictable. You can confidently say "Q4_K_M of Llama-3-8B loses roughly 1–2 points on MMLU vs. FP16."
- **MoE models quantize in a more fragile way.** Each expert saw fewer tokens during training (only the tokens routed to it), so individual experts are less robust to low-precision rounding. In practice Q4 and Q8 of MoE models still work acceptably, but the quality cliff can appear earlier than in a dense model of the same active size. The shared components (attention, embeddings, router) quantize normally; the experts are the weak point.
- The practical trap: to fit a MoE model in the same RAM as a dense model, you must quantize **more total parameters**, often at a lower bit-width, to compensate for the larger weight count. You end up with a more aggressively quantized model that may not actually be better than the dense alternative.

## Quality per parameter

This is the one axis where MoE genuinely wins, but the right denominator matters:

| Metric | Dense | MoE |
|---|---|---|
| Quality per **active** parameter | baseline | **~1.5–2× better** (the main selling point) |
| Quality per **total** parameter | baseline | worse (you pay storage/compute for idle experts) |
| Quality per **byte of RAM** | **better** (all params are active) | worse (most params are idle but still resident) |
| Quality per **token of latency** | better at batch=1 | marginally better if fully resident, worse if offloaded |

For a local device, the binding constraint is bytes of RAM, not FLOPs. So the metric that matters is **quality per byte**, and that favours dense.

## A concrete illustration

Suppose you have 16 GB of usable RAM and want an interactive assistant:

- **Dense path:** Llama-3-8B at Q4_K_M (~5 GB weights) + KV cache + context. Fits comfortably. You get solid 8B-class quality with predictable ~20–40 tok/s on a modern CPU or ~80+ tok/s on a discrete GPU.
- **MoE path:** Mixtral 8×7B at Q4 (~65 GB). Doesn't fit. You'd need to offload ~5 experts to disk, accepting latency spikes. Or you drop to Q2, which degrades quality badly. You're stuck.

At 32 GB you can load a Q4 Mixtral and get near-70B-dense quality with 13B-active compute. That's the regime where MoE becomes attractive locally.

---

## Recommendation for an interactive assistant

**Default to a dense model.** For the vast majority of memory-constrained local setups (8–24 GB), a well-quantized dense 7–14B model (Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-14B, Mistral-7B) gives you:

- predictable, low variance latency,
- well-understood quantization behaviour,
- the best quality-per-byte you can get in that memory tier,
- a simpler deployment story (no routing, no expert-cache management).

**Reach for MoE only when three conditions are met simultaneously:**

1. You have enough RAM (typically ≥ 32 GB) to keep the full expert pool resident at Q4 or better.
2. Your workload is latency-tolerant enough that the slightly higher memory footprint is acceptable (you're not on a laptop with 16 GB shared with the OS and a browser).
3. You've benchmarked and confirmed the quality gain over the best dense model that fits in the same memory is meaningful for *your* tasks.

If you're on a 16 GB laptop, a Q4 dense 8B model will almost always feel better (faster, more reliable, less RAM pressure) than a half-offloaded MoE model that occasionally stutters. The interactive-assistant use case punishes latency variance more than it rewards a 5% quality bump.

**Practical decision procedure:**

1. Measure your usable RAM after OS, GUI, and other apps. Subtract ~2–4 GB for KV cache and runtime overhead.
2. Find the largest dense model that fits at Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M. Benchmark it on your actual assistant tasks.
3. Only then check whether a MoE model whose *total* weight size fits in that budget offers a meaningful quality improvement. If it doesn't fit without offloading, skip it.
4. If you're at the 32 GB+ tier and the MoE model fits fully resident, A/B test it against your dense baseline on real prompts. The quality-per-active-parameter advantage is real, but it's not always enough to justify the memory cost for a casual assistant.

**Memory:**
- Dense model: all parameters are loaded and active in every forward pass. Memory footprint = model size (plus KV cache, activations).
- MoE model: total parameter count is much larger, but only a subset of experts is activated per token. The key question for local inference is: do you need to load ALL experts into memory, or can you keep them on disk and stream them in?
  - If you load all experts into RAM (the typical case for local inference with a fixed memory budget), the MoE model has a much larger memory footprint than a dense model of comparable "active" parameters. E.g., Mixtral 8x7B has ~129B total params but ~13B active. You need ~130GB to load it all (or ~65GB at Q4). A dense 13B model needs ~8GB at Q4.
  - The "trick" some people use: keep experts on disk and load the active ones per token. But this creates massive I/O latency and is impractical for interactive use unless you have very fast NVMe and the routing is predictable.
  - So for a memory-constrained device, MoE is actually a disadvantage in raw memory unless you're doing expert offloading/streaming, which hurts latency.

**Latency:**
- Dense: predictable latency, all params read from memory per token. Memory bandwidth is the bottleneck.
- MoE: fewer active params per token, so in theory less compute and less memory bandwidth per token. BUT you still need to have all experts resident in memory (or stream them). If all experts are in memory, the latency per token is lower than a dense model of the same total size, but comparable to a dense model of the same active size. The routing adds a small overhead.
- The real latency issue: if you can only fit a subset of experts in memory, you get I/O stalls. For interactive use (low latency, high responsiveness), this is bad.
- MoE can have higher variance in latency because different tokens route to different experts, causing cache misses.

**Quantization behaviour:**
- Dense models: well-studied quantization. Q4_K_M, Q5, Q8 work well. Quality degradation is relatively predictable.
- MoE models: quantization is trickier. Experts are sparse-activated, so each expert sees fewer tokens during training. This means:
  - Individual experts may be less "robust" to quantization because they've seen less data.
  - But in practice, MoE models quantize reasonably well at Q4-Q8. The issue is more about the absolute memory: you need to quantize MORE parameters to get the same active capacity.
  - There's also the issue that quantization error compounds differently: in a dense model, every layer's error affects every token uniformly. In MoE, only the routed experts' errors affect a given token, so the effective quantization noise per token might be lower (fewer sources of error contributing). But this is a second-order effect.
  - The practical issue: to fit a MoE model in the same memory as a dense model, you need to quantize the MoE more aggressively, which hurts quality.

**Quality per parameter:**
- "Per active parameter": MoE models generally achieve higher quality per active parameter than dense models. This is the main selling point. Mixtral 8x7B (13B active) beats Llama-3-8B and is competitive with Llama-3-70B on some benchmarks.
- "Per total parameter": MoE is less efficient per total parameter. You're paying for parameters you don't use on any given token.
- For local inference, the relevant metric is "quality per byte of memory" or "quality per token of latency." Here MoE has a disadvantage because you need to store all experts.
- However, if you have enough memory to load the full MoE model, you get better quality per active parameter, which translates to better quality per token of compute.

**Practical recommendation for interactive assistant:**
- Interactive assistant = low latency required (ideally < 200ms per token or < 1-2 seconds for a full response), memory constrained (maybe 8-32GB RAM).
- For most memory-constrained local setups (8-16GB), a dense model is the safer choice. You get predictable latency, well-understood quantization, and you can fit a model that's "good enough."
- MoE makes sense when: you have enough memory to load the full model (e.g., 32GB+ for a Q4 Mixtral), you want the quality boost per active parameter, and you can tolerate slightly higher memory usage.
- The "sweet spot" for local interactive use is often a dense 7-14B model at Q4-Q8.
- MoE becomes attractive at the 32-64GB memory tier where you can load a full MoE model and get near-70B quality with 13B active compute.

Let me also think about:
- KV cache: both have KV cache overhead. MoE doesn't reduce KV cache (attention is still dense in most MoE architectures).
- Batch processing: MoE can be more efficient at higher batch sizes because different tokens can use different experts. But for interactive (batch=1), this advantage is minimal.
- Speculative decoding: works for both, but the interaction with MoE routing is more complex.
